title: What Defiles, and Crumbs for the Nations
summary: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem challenge Jesus because his disciples eat without the ritual handwashing of tradition, and he answers that they break God's command to keep their traditions and that defilement comes from the heart. In the region of Tyre and Sidon a Canaanite woman persists in asking for her daughter's healing until Jesus praises her great faith. Back by the Sea of Galilee he heals many and feeds four thousand men, besides women and children.
story: Jesus' reputation has now reached Jerusalem, the center of religious authority, and a delegation comes north to question him. The conflict moves from the Sabbath (chapter 12) to purity and tradition, and Jesus' answer goes to the root of the matter: the heart. Then, as if to act out what he has just taught about clean and unclean, he goes into Gentile territory and meets a woman whose ancestry made her doubly an outsider. Her faith is the second example in Matthew, after the centurion in chapter 8, of a Gentile whose trust outstrips that of Israel's leaders. The second feeding, which follows, shows that the bread of the kingdom is abundant enough for more than one table.
historical:
The tradition of the elders was the body of oral teaching the Pharisees had developed to apply the law of Moses to daily life. The Pharisees believed these traditions guarded the written law and made holiness possible for ordinary people, not only priests; the Sadducees, the priestly aristocracy, rejected them. Much of this tradition was later written down in the Mishnah around AD 200. Ritual handwashing before meals was one such practice, drawn from the purity rules for priests eating holy food and extended by Pharisees to ordinary meals. The concern was ritual purity, not hygiene.

The practice described in verses 5 and 6 is the one Mark 7:11 calls Corban, a Hebrew word for an offering. A person could declare property devoted to God, which put it beyond use for other purposes, including the support of aged parents. Later rabbinic writings show that teachers themselves debated when such vows could be released. Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician cities on the coast north of Galilee, outside Jewish territory. Mark 7:26 describes the woman as a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth; Matthew's term Canaanite recalls the ancient inhabitants of the land whom Israel displaced, a word with centuries of hostility behind it. Magadan (verse 39) is unknown; it may be another name for Magdala on the west shore, and Mark 8:10 names Dalmanutha instead.
cultural:
Purity in Jewish life marked the boundary between common and holy, deciding who could enter the temple and eat holy food, and which foods, contacts, and conditions made a person ritually unclean. Food laws (Leviticus 11) also marked Israel off from other nations. For Jesus to say that nothing entering the mouth defiles a person struck at a central marker of Jewish identity; Mark 7:19 draws the conclusion that he declared all foods clean, while Matthew keeps the focus on handwashing.

Honoring father and mother, the fifth commandment, included supporting parents in old age, a serious duty in a world without pensions. Dogs in Jewish usage were generally unclean scavengers, and dog was a term of contempt some Jews used for Gentiles. The word in verses 26 and 27, kunarion, is a diminutive, which may point to household dogs under the table, and the woman takes the image up in exactly that sense. A crowd staying three days in the countryside would have exhausted any food they brought. The seven baskets of verse 37 are a different word (spuris) from the twelve baskets of 14:20; it describes a large hamper, of the kind in which Paul was lowered over the wall of Damascus in Acts 9:25.
literary: The chapter moves from debate to parable to miracle. Verses 1 to 20 are a controversy in three scenes: Jesus answers the leaders with a counter-question and Scripture (verses 3 to 9), declares a principle to the crowd (verses 10 and 11), and explains it privately to the disciples (verses 12 to 20). The list of evils from the heart in verse 19 follows the order of the commandments (murder, adultery, theft, false witness). The Canaanite woman's story is built on refusals: silence, the disciples' request to send her away, a statement of Jesus' mission to Israel, and the saying about dogs. Each refusal is met by her persistence, and the scene turns on her reply. The feeding of the four thousand (verses 32 to 39) is told with deliberate echoes of the five thousand in chapter 14, and Jesus will refer to both in 16:9-10.

outline.t: The tradition of the elders and the command of God
Many healed by the Sea of Galilee

doctrines.note: Jesus locates the source of evil not in outside contamination but in the human heart, from which come evil thoughts and every kind of wrong. Religious practice that only guards the outside leaves the real problem untouched.
Jesus distinguishes God's command from human tradition and refuses to let the second overrule the first. He quotes Isaiah 29:13 against worship that honors God with lips while the heart is far away.

The Canaanite woman's faith is humble, persistent, and sharp. She accepts her place as an outsider but believes there is enough mercy in Jesus even for crumbs to heal her daughter. Jesus calls her faith great.

Jesus' mission is first to the lost sheep of Israel, yet a Gentile receives healing and, in the verses that follow, crowds glorify the God of Israel. The chapter anticipates the mission to all nations that Jesus commands in 28:19.

words.note: Paradosis, tradition, literally something handed over. It can be positive (Paul uses it for the apostolic teaching he passed on, as in 2 Thessalonians 2:15) or negative, as here, when human additions come to override God's command. The issue is not tradition as such but its authority relative to God's word.

Koinoo, to make common or defile. In Jewish usage common meant not set apart as holy, and so ritually unclean. Jesus uses the word five times in verses 11, 18, and 20 to redefine where defilement really comes from.

Kunarion, a little dog or house dog, a diminutive of the usual word for dog. Whether the diminutive softens the image is debated, but the woman seizes on it: house dogs are under the table, and they eat what falls.

Chananaios, Canaanite. It is the only use of the word in the New Testament. By choosing this old name rather than Mark's Syrophoenician, Matthew underlines how far outside Israel she stands, and so how far Jesus' mercy reaches.

christ: Jesus speaks here as the one who can distinguish God's will from human additions and read the law at its deepest intent, a role the prophets played and that he claims with his own authority. The Canaanite woman addresses him as Lord and Son of David, the Messiah of Israel, and he acts as Israel's Messiah whose blessing flows out to the nations, fulfilling God's promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3). The healings by the lake echo Isaiah 35, where the lame leap and the mute sing when God comes to save, and the crowds glorify the God of Israel. The second feeding shows the Shepherd of chapter 14 again providing bread in the wilderness, and the pattern of taking, giving thanks, breaking, and giving points ahead to the Last Supper.

hard.q: Why does Jesus first ignore the Canaanite woman and then seem to compare her to a dog?
hard.a: This is one of the most uncomfortable scenes in the Gospels. Jesus' silence, his statement that he was sent only to Israel, and his saying about the children's bread and the dogs sound harsh. Interpreters have offered several readings. Some emphasize salvation history: Jesus' earthly mission was genuinely focused on Israel first, as in 10:5-6, and the saying states that priority plainly; the woman accepts it and still asks, and her faith opens the door that will fully open after the resurrection. Others see Jesus testing and drawing out her faith, much as a teacher presses a student, knowing how she will answer; the diminutive word for dog and the image of a household table leave room for her reply. Some modern interpreters argue that Jesus himself is shown moving, in his human experience, toward a wider view of his mission through this encounter; others reject this as inconsistent with Matthew's portrait. All agree on the outcome: Jesus praises her faith as great, heals her daughter, and in Matthew's arrangement the scene answers the question about clean and unclean that opens the chapter. Readers need not smooth over the harshness to see where the story lands.

questions: Jesus accused the Pharisees of honoring God with their lips while their hearts were far away. Where might that describe your own worship?
What traditions, good in themselves, have you seen become more important than love for God or neighbor?
The Canaanite woman kept asking despite silence and refusal. What does her persistence teach you about prayer when God seems silent?
